item.title: C.E.O.s Say the A.I. Rollout Is Going Well. Employees Feel Differently.
item.description:
By Jordyn Holman

When it comes to artificial intelligence, chief executives and their work forces aren’t seeing eye to eye.

Corporate leaders, increasingly in earnings calls and interviews, tout productivity gains and say they are doing right by their workers as they roll out the technology.

But workers are much more concerned about being supplanted, and they don’t trust their company’s executives.

A survey from the Milken Institute-Harris Poll Listening Project recently found that more than two-thirds of business leaders expect they will be better off financially in five years because of A.I., while just 27 percent of the U.S. work force felt the same way — a whopping 41 point gap.

Workers also see less A.I. transformation than leadership does. Nearly three-fourths of leaders say A.I. has significantly changed the way work is done, compared with 58 percent of entry and midlevel employees, according to a report released this month from the Wharton School.

“We have corner offices and cubicles, driving the same economy, but living in completely different realities,” John Gerzema, C.E.O. of the Harris Poll, said in an email. “There is a gulf in hope between what leaders think A.I. could bring to companies and what employees feel it is taking away from them.”

What might be worse is that C.E.O.s don’t seem to recognize the disconnect, or that they’re losing the trust of their workers.

For example: Just 15 percent of C.E.O.s said they were concerned about how their approach to A.I. could erode their employees’ trust, according to a survey released this month by consultancy BCG. But 40 percent of workers said their C.E.O. has not been transparent enough about the impact of A.I. on their role and career trajectory.

The distrust doesn’t make for a successful transformation, said Julia Dhar, the leader of the North American people and organization practice at BCG and an author of the study.

“You will not get the people you need to start using it more intensively to do so,” Dhar said. “And there is a very good chance you will get backsliding or regression from other people.”

Hemant Taneja, who leads the venture capital firm General Catalyst, said the findings of the BCG report were not surprising, but relatable.

“When there’s more ambiguity, you need to over-communicate,” Taneja said in an interview. “I’m feeling the pain of that in my own business as well.”

He said he has been working to build trust by explaining his decisions around A.I. to employees and founders, especially when they change.

“You have to be vulnerable about the fact that we don’t have all the answers,” Taneja said. “We directionally know where to go, but we don’t know all the answers, and so it’s OK to change assumptions and change your mind.” Dhar said one C.E.O. she knows starts frank discussions around A.I. by asking his frontline employees, “What is the silliest thing we do at this company?” This approach works, she said, because it’s not judgmental, and the C.E.O. doesn’t have to agree on it or make a promise to look into it further.

“But you’ve given people a really easy way to make their voice heard,” she said.

Tim Walsh, chief executive of consultancy KPMG, says when he travels to offices in different cities he makes a point to sit down with both the partners in the business as well as employees.

“I need to understand how they’re feeling, I need to understand how the technology is being received and I need to understand their concerns,” Walsh said in an interview. “I will tell you it’s hard to get it at my level.”

Walsh said he hasn’t mastered the art of getting rank-and-file employees to open up completely in front of him. KPMG relies on anonymous employee surveys as a platform where more junior employees can feel freer to complain.

Despite a struggle to build trust with workers around A.I., there is a bright spot for chief executives. The distrust Americans have toward C.E.O.s and more specifically their own C.E.O. is less than it is for other institutions in American life like media outlets, NGOs and government, according to the Edelman Trust Barometer, which has been measuring trust levels in for the past 26 years.

The research also found that U.S. employees appreciated hearing from their leaders about A.I. even in instances when they didn’t have all the answers.

“People are often very realistic about a business reality and their requests are often quite humble,” Dhar said. “They say, I would just hope the leaders are able to be honest and specific about the changes that we are making and the reason behind them.”

Tesla and SpaceX are considering a merger. Elon Musk confirmed on Tuesday that the boards of each company have formed a special committee to explore a tie-up. Musk cautioned that any such proposal would require approval from at least 50 percent of all outstanding shares in Tesla.

Researchers discovered a widespread security vulnerability. Companies and government agencies scrambled to patch the major bug in PHP, an open-source programming language that is critical to internet architecture. The vulnerability was detected with the help of A.I., but bad actors could also use A.I. to exploit it.

Mark Zuckerberg struck a deal to pay California’s potential billionaire tax. Zuckerberg negotiated with the company’s board over how he would pay the one-time 5 percent tax on all holdings. Meta responded by creating a new class of shares that allows him to raise billions without compromising his voting power in the company. In return, he agreed to stay in the state for eight more years, except for under some conditions. The new share class will also let Meta raise more money for its A.I. ambitions.

More big deals: Saudi Arabia postponed its big investment conference amid concerns about security. Trump asked Elon Musk to restore Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite communications network. And next week will be a big test for the strength of A.I. financing: Anthropic is expected to file its public I.P.O. prospectus within the next few days, and Google, Microsoft and Amazon report earnings.

Meta’s new A.I. team has 50 engineers for every manager. Airbnb’s C.E.O., Brian Chesky, has popularized the delegation-shunning strategy of staying in “founders mode.” While Uber, Meta, Amazon and more have been aggressively laying off middle managers.

In the midst of what has been termed “the Great Flattening,” hierarchy seems to have few defenders. But Nir Halevy, a professor of organizational behavior at Stanford University, argues that levels of management are actually quite useful — when done right. He talked with Sarah Kessler about his new book, “Level Up.” The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Why don’t flat organizations work?

It’s difficult to scale. And we all engage in social comparisons. Those tendencies don’t disappear just because we decided to create a flat structure.

There’s a lot of evidence showing that informal hierarchies are very swift and powerful in the tendency to emerge.

What do you want instead of an informal hierarchy?

You want it to be based on common values. We want to create a hierarchy that provides people with multiple pathways to contribute and thrive and ascend and lead.

What usually makes the hierarchy dysfunctional?

One, if they’re ultracompetitive. And that competition might manifest in withholding help or may actually lead to sabotage.

Broken hierarchies are unjust. You really deserve a promotion, but you’re not going to get the promotion because the boss’s nephew got it. You get arbitrary decisions that are not justified and not explained.

And instability. You will experience a lot of unpredictable, swift changes. People leave, there is a lot of turnover, retention becomes a struggle and people feel a sense of threat and stress and paranoia.

Is there a size at which you don’t need hierarchy?

One of the examples I discuss in the book is Valve, which makes video games and has a few hundred employees. It presents itself to the world as a flat organization. If you go to their landing page, they say, We’ve been boss free since 1996. But they do distinguish based on salaries. They are not all receiving the same information. They have informal hierarchies.

But if I have just like 10 people, is it reasonable to say I’m the boss, but everybody else is on the same level?

You can say that. The question is the extent to which the people actually think that it’s true or fair.

Does A.I. change hierarchy? Do we still need middle management?

Initiatives to use technology to flatten organizations are definitely on the rise. But there is a neglect of the multiple functions that people, let’s say middle management, are doing.

If people erroneously believe their managers are only aggregating information from the bottom, transferring it upward, or taking kind of directions from the top and transferring it downward, then they might mistakenly believe that A.I. can replace employees.

This question comes from a recent edition of the newsletter. Click an answer to see if you’re right. (The link is free.)

A.I. music is flooding onto music streaming platforms. Which of the following listening services bans it?

Bandcamp

Apple Music

Spotify

All of the above

Thanks for reading! We’ll see you Monday.

We’d like your feedback. Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

Follow DealBook on Instagram: @nytdealbook

item.title: Noah Adams, Longtime Host of ‘All Things Considered,’ Has Died at 84
item.description:
Noah Adams, a longtime host of NPR’s “All Things Considered” whose quiet baritone and empathetic ear brought listeners stories of back-roads America not often heard on the national airwaves, died on Oct. 16 at his home in Yellow Springs, Ohio. He was 84.

The cause was complications of a benign brain tumor removed eight years ago, his wife, Neenah Ellis, said.

Mr. Adams was a postman’s son from Kentucky who never finished college, and he worked hard to lose the Appalachian accent that he knew conjured up negative stereotypes about his native region.

But he never lost his respect for rural and working-class Americans, and he delighted in leaving Washington, where NPR is based, to travel around the country interviewing miners, farmers, single mothers and factory workers.

In the morning meetings, where the day’s events and newsmakers were discussed, Ms. Ellis, who worked in production at NPR, recalled, “He was looking for who was yearning, who was in pain, who needed help out in the country.”

Mr. Adams abhorred interviewing officials with pat talking points, though that was often part of his job as host of the weeknight edition of “All Things Considered,” NPR’s flagship news and interview show, a position he held for 18 years. He preferred to seek out regular people whose lives were affected by national events.

“The best stories come from west of the Potomac,” he once said.

His respect for his sources came through in interviews of those unaccustomed to a microphone.

“He was wonderfully warm and conversational with people,” said Melissa Block, another host of “All Things Considered,” who worked as a producer for Mr. Adams early in her career. “I don’t know that anyone talking with him would think, ‘Oh, the interview is about to start.’ It would just be a conversation.”

From 1982 to 1987, Mr. Adams’s co-host on “All Things Considered” was Susan Stamberg, an emotive, brainy New Yorker. It was a matchup that showed how opposites attract.

“He is the most genuine, uncontrived voice in broadcasting,” Ms. Stamberg wrote in the introduction to a 1992 book that Mr. Adams wrote about a year of his work for NPR.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

After a short hiatus, he returned to host “All Things Considered” with Robert Siegel and Linda Wertheimer from 1989 until 2002.

“He was a very private and shy person,” Mr. Siegel said in an interview.

After Mr. Adams wrote a book about learning to play the piano at 51, “Piano Lessons” (1997), Mr. Siegel recalled Mr. Adams’s distress at realizing that he would have to perform on his book tour: “I watched him at a Borders, and he was terrified. But he loved what he did. He pulled it off very beautifully.”

During his time away from NPR, from 1987 to 1989, Mr. Adams was recruited to host a replacement show for the much-loved “A Prairie Home Companion,” whose creator, Garrison Keillor, had left. The replacement, “Good Evening,” was another folksy variety show broadcast live from a theater in St. Paul, Minn. It was enlivened by Mr. Adams’s essays about the community on the St. Croix River where he had settled, but it struggled to replicate Mr. Keillor’s audience.

The show lasted less than a year, and Mr. Adams announced his departure shortly before it ended. “I never felt people were saying, ‘Gee, that’s not Garrison Keillor,’” he later said somewhat defensively.

Noah Donald Adams was born on Sept. 15, 1942, in Ashland, Ky., the elder of fraternal twin boys. His father, Roy Adams, and his mother, Edith (Wellman) Adams, a secretary, divorced soon after, and Noah and his brother, James, were raised by their mother and maternal grandparents.

Noah graduated from Ashland High School (now Paul G. Blazer High School) and attended Eastern Kentucky State College (now Eastern Kentucky University) for 18 months before being asked to leave because he was living in unauthorized off-campus housing and writing term papers for football players.

He knocked around doing various jobs, — including construction and car sales, before joining the University of Kentucky’s public radio station, WBKY (now WUKY), in Lexington. There, he hosted a progressive rock show and worked the control board for other shows.

After writing a letter to NPR, he was hired in 1975 as a production assistant on “All Things Considered,” which had been introduced four years earlier. In 1978, he became a weekend co-host for the show.

A 90-minute documentary that he co-wrote about the mass suicide at Jonestown in Guyana in 1978, “Father Cares: The Last of Jonestown” (1981), received wide notice for its innovative format and subject. It was based on 900 hours of recordings that the cult leader Jim Jones and his followers had made before their deaths. Mr. Jones’s voice was so chilling, The Minneapolis Star Tribune noted, that “a listener might cling to the rational tone of narrator Noah Adams as to the hand of a friend.”

Though he preferred feature reporting, Mr. Adams did not shy away from hard news at home or abroad. He won an award from the Overseas Press Club of America in 1994 for work he did in Serbia on the roots of the country’s national extremism.

On Sept. 11, 2001, he was on the air from the morning until after dark, updating millions of listeners about the terrorist attacks. He called it the most important day of his career, when he could “feel the audience” intent on understanding the shocking events, Ms. Ellis said.

The following year, Mr. Adams took a leave of absence to research a book about the Wright brothers, one of five nonfiction books he wrote. When he returned, it was as a contributing correspondent on NPR’s national desk. He roamed widely but regularly returned to stories in Appalachia.

Ms. Ellis, who married Mr. Adams in 1987, recalled visiting Appalachia for the first time with him. They were on assignment — she was his producer — and he instructed her and an engineer on how to approach strangers wary of outsiders. You don’t knock on their doors, he told them: “You drive up, get out of the car and stand there until they come out.”

Mr. Adams’s first two marriages ended in divorce. In addition to Ms. Ellis, he is survived by his brother.

Among the thousands of stories that Mr. Adams reported, the one that got the most enthusiastic response was when he visited a New York recording studio and sang a wobbly version of the Eagles song “Take It to the Limit.”

He played the tape on the air for Ms. Stamberg, who squealed, “It’s adorable!”

One of the hundreds of listeners who wrote in said, “I was getting ready to drop out of law school and we were thinking about getting a divorce, but if you have the courage to stand in that studio and play it for Susan on the radio, then I know we can do anything we really set our minds to.”

item.title: Audi to Build Factory in Georgia, Trump Says
item.description:
Audi, Volkswagen’s luxury car division, plans to build a factory in Georgia, its first in the United States, President Trump said at a rally in the state on Saturday.

A factory in the United States would help Volkswagen and Audi reduce their exposure to Mr. Trump’s 25 percent import tariffs on foreign vehicles and auto parts that have been deadly for sales. Audi imports all the vehicles it sells in the United States from factories in Europe or Mexico.

Volkswagen has a factory in Chattanooga, Tenn., but produces only one model there, the Atlas sport utility vehicle. Other Volkswagen models are imported, in many cases from Mexico.

Audi will invest $4 billion in the factory south of Macon, which will be able to produce 200,000 vehicles a year, Georgia officials said. Audi will begin grading earth at the site this year but it will not reach full production until 2031.

Mr. Trump portrayed the investment as a sign that his tariffs, which economists have said are inflationary, had inspired Audi’s decision. “Without tariffs, they would not have been coming in,” Mr. Trump said.

Audi will produce sport utility vehicles at the site, Gernot Döllner, the head of Audi, said after being called to the stage by Mr. Trump.

BMW and Mercedes-Benz, Audi’s main rivals, have long had factories in the United States — BMW in South Carolina and Mercedes in Alabama — where they mainly produce sport utility vehicles.

By promising to invest in a key battleground state, and giving Mr. Trump something to brag about, Volkswagen may be hoping to win concessions from the White House that would lower the tariff burden and help the company revive flagging sales in the United States.

“We can do something with you because you’re building your cars in the United States,” Mr. Trump said.

Sales of Volkswagen cars in the United States, including the Audi and Porsche brands, slumped almost 10 percent in the third quarter, according to estimates by Cox Automotive. With a market share of 3.4 percent, Volkswagen is a minor player in the United States even though it is the second-largest carmaker worldwide after Toyota.

The German carmaker has been trying for decades to increase its sales in the United States to a level commensurate with its global stature. The United States is particularly attractive because it is one of the few markets where there is no competition from Chinese carmakers. Chinese cars are effectively barred from the United States by tariffs of more than 100 percent.

Volkswagen is already building a factory in South Carolina to manufacture pickups and sport utility vehicles using the Scout brand beginning next year.

Such projects are risky. Automakers including Volkswagen are already burdened with underused factories that weigh on profits. Volkswagen, which has lost market share in Europe to Chinese automakers like BYD and Geely, has said that it may need to close or sell four factories in Europe.

Richard Fausset contributed reporting.

item.title: How to Straddle the MAGA Divide
item.description:
Just after 11 a.m. on Oct. 6, a voice of the Trump resistance filled Courtroom 21 of the federal district courthouse in Washington, D.C.

Beth Wilkinson, a prominent trial lawyer, was speaking before a judge on behalf of Disney and its ABC network against what she said was a brazen attempt by the Trump administration to hobble a free press: an unscheduled review of ABC’s broadcasting licenses that could eventually force its eight directly owned stations off the air. The network regarded the review as payback for its critical programming, especially jokes by the late-night host Jimmy Kimmel that upset President Trump.

Ms. Wilkinson argued that the mere threat of lost licenses meant editorial decision makers were strapped to a guillotine, weighing every word with the blade hanging over their necks. She portrayed the president as a kind of mafioso-in-chief intent on using the government to settle grudges and scores. “He now has control of vast regulatory powers that he’s willing to unleash against people or organizations who exercise First Amendment speech that he does not like,” she told the judge.

Ms. Wilkinson’s tone may have been cutting and her metaphors hyperbolic, but she is not exactly a staple of the “no kings” circuit.

A former Justice Department official, Ms. Wilkinson has represented Democratic politicians facing sexual harassment or assault allegations and helped guide Justice Brett Kavanaugh through his messy Supreme Court confirmation fight. She has defended tobacco companies and drugmakers; she helped the National Football League fight concussion-related suits from ex-players and Microsoft defeat a Biden-era antitrust lawsuit.

Earlier this year, the media mogul who controls Paramount, David Ellison, hired her to defend his $111 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery against an attempt by state attorneys general to derail it. Mr. Ellison’s father, Larry, a founder of Oracle, is close to the Trump administration, which had already blessed the merger.

Ms. Wilkinson is arguably the most influential current example of a venerable type: the Washington lawyer who can operate on both sides of a divide. The type was epitomized by Edward Bennett Williams, who represented both Senator Joe McCarthy, the notorious Communist-hunter, and Hollywood screenwriters accused of Communist activities. Williams later founded the firm Williams & Connolly and famously advised A-listers of both parties. The political agility only cemented his status as one of the wise elders of Washington.

Today, however, the mood has shifted. The differences between parties are no longer merely about policy or even ideology. Democrats say Mr. Trump is destroying free speech, the rule of law and other bedrocks of democracy, while the president’s allies insist deep-state prosecutors and left-wing college professors initiated the assault. The stakes feel existential.

“The only way to switch sides at this point is to become a total apostate,” said Lee Drutman, a political scientist who has studied the influence industry in Washington. “If the narrative from Democrats is that Republicans are not only different but evil, and vice versa, that’s a very different set of conflicts.”

Which raises a question for advocates like Beth Wilkinson: Does the Trump era mark the high point of the Washington superlawyer, by underscoring the value of Beltway actors who can toggle between MAGA acolytes and enemies? Or, in an age when each side is more fevered and less tolerant of disloyalty, is the situationally flexible Washington lawyer on the verge of extinction?

A Navy captain’s daughter who attended Princeton on an R.O.T.C. scholarship, Ms. Wilkinson was working in the Justice Department in 1995 on the day of a massive bombing in Oklahoma City. She was eager to work on the case and, when an opportunity arose, rushed to persuade her boss, Merrick Garland, to sign off.

“I sat outside Merrick’s door till he’d see me, begging to go,” she said in an interview. “I would have emptied the trash cans to be on that case.” Despite being the youngest prosecutor at the counsel table, she wound up handling the closing argument for the death-penalty sentencing of the convicted bomber, Timothy McVeigh.

Ms. Wilkinson left government work not long after, figuring she would make a brief stop in private practice to earn some money. A brief stint as general counsel of the troubled mortgage finance company Fannie Mae ended with a minor thud when the government took it over and she and other top executives resigned in 2008. (She arrived after the company’s accounting issues became public.) But she was being hailed by colleagues and clients more often than not, and developing a very specific reputation — as the lawyer a business hires after it decides to fight rather than settle.

To young lawyers who struggled with the ethics of representing corporate defendants, Ms. Wilkinson offered a helpful mental exercise. She would acknowledge the temptation to dismiss clients like tobacco companies as beyond the pale. But she emphasized that many defendants are more complicated than they first appear.

“She said, be open to working on a case you might think is morally reprehensible for some reasons, you might turn out to have a different perspective on them,” recalled Cali Arat, who worked as a summer associate at the firm Paul Weiss, where Ms. Wilkinson was a partner. “I had gone to Macalester College, a liberal school. It was the first time someone presented it that way.”

Ms. Wilkinson had developed a network among Democratic big shots partly through her work at the Justice Department — Mr. Garland later officiated at her marriage to David Gregory, the television journalist — and by 2015 had begun to take on political clients, too. Among them were aides to Hillary Clinton caught up in an F.B.I. investigation of a private email server and a congressional investigation of Benghazi, Libya.

She took the cases with her as she left Paul Weiss to start her own firm the following year. But Ms. Wilkinson was keen to represent more than just Democrats in good standing. She had long admired Williams & Connolly, the politically ambidextrous law firm that rarely turned away a client tainted by scandal. One of the firm’s partners defended President Bill Clinton during his impeachment proceedings, as well as Mr. Trump during the first-term Russia investigation.

Ms. Wilkinson got her chance to hone that approach a few years later, when Mr. Kavanaugh asked her to help navigate his bumpy Supreme Court confirmation process. Facing accusations of sexual assault or misconduct, Mr. Kavanaugh was the kind of client she might have had to turn away at a large, risk-averse firm.

Now, she could essentially override her colleagues’ misgivings. She called a meeting of the roughly 40 lawyers at the firm and informed them she was taking the job, though she said she wouldn’t force any associate to work on the matter if he or she felt uncomfortable doing so.

“She fundamentally believes, and as a former public defender I’ve always believed, that everyone deserves representation, particularly in the face of government overreach,” said Brian Stekloff, the other named partner at Ms. Wilkinson’s firm.

As a business move, the Kavanaugh episode appeared to be a success. Ms. Wilkinson was all over television news, where potential clients could see that she was a relentless advocate, unafraid of controversy. “I think she’s always wanted to take the biggest case of the moment if she can be involved in it,” said Ms. Arat, now a partner at Wilkinson Stekloff. “The Kavanaugh thing was a huge deal.”

But at times, the matter seemed to test her ease at squaring the job with her moral intuitions. After Ms. Wilkinson raised doubts about one Kavanaugh accuser on CNN by questioning why the woman’s lawyer hadn’t reported her allegations to the police, Wolf Blitzer pointed out that women often don’t come forward to report sexual assault because they feel degraded and embarrassed.

Ms. Wilkinson, who had helped found an organization to promote female lawyers, agreed. “It is one of the few good things that’s happened in this country in the last few years — that the Me Too movement has come out and women have been able to speak up,” she responded.

Then she added, “It’s also important that everyone gets a defense, and gets to face those accusations fairly.”

Ms. Wilkinson told me that, “to an outsider, it can look contradictory. But it’s possible for both to be true at the same time.”

Not everyone was persuaded. In late 2019, the firm received a public rebuke of sorts when Pete Buttigieg’s presidential campaign said it would return a political donation from Ms. Wilkinson and one of her partners. A Buttigieg spokesperson told The Guardian that Mr. Kavanaugh “should have never been put on the Supreme Court, and this campaign will not accept donations from those who played a role in making that happen.”

This summer Ms. Wilkinson got a call from David Ellison, the tech scion and owner of Paramount, asking if she would work with Mr. Ellison’s parent company on its acquisition of Warner Bros. His company was fighting a coalition of state attorneys general who opposed the deal on antitrust grounds, and the judge seemed sympathetic to some of their claims.

Mr. Ellison and his executives had taken notice of Ms. Wilkinson’s courtroom successes over government lawyers, including a win for Microsoft that cleared the way for its $70 billion purchase of the video game giant Activision Blizzard.

But the case also raised political questions that went beyond mergers and acquisitions. In 2025, Paramount had paid Mr. Trump $16 million to settle what was widely seen as a frivolous lawsuit against “60 Minutes,” which appeared to clinch the administration’s backing for the purchase of the storied media company. It looked to many outside MAGA like a quid pro quo, though Paramount said there was no connection. Mr. Ellison denied having anything to do with the settlement.

Ms. Wilkinson, for her part, looked nothing like an anti-Trump fulminator. “There aren’t many Democrat attorneys who are effective like her,” said Mike Davis, a former Republican Senate aide who helped oversee Mr. Kavanaugh’s nomination process. “She doesn’t have a problem in Trump world — she was so good on Kavanaugh. Other Democrats wouldn’t be able to navigate it.”

Mr. Davis, who runs a firm that helps companies win approval for mergers pending before the administration, among other matters, said he had personally recommended Ms. Wilkinson to corporate clients seeking a trial lawyer. (The Warner Bros. deal ultimately closed this month, after the company settled with the state attorneys general and avoided a trial.)

The bipartisan cred has even prompted some clients to seek out Ms. Wilkinson when they plan to, in effect, plead for mercy with the administration. After the Justice Department began an inquiry into diversity and inclusion practices at the University of Virginia last year, the university’s board hired Ms. Wilkinson to handle its dealings with the school’s president, James Ryan.

Board members believed the university had legal exposure stemming from a lack of compliance with a Supreme Court ruling on affirmative action, according to a person familiar with the situation who was not authorized to discuss the case. They worried that the Trump administration would treat the school harshly if Mr. Ryan stayed on. But Mr. Ryan was skeptical that the school had violated the ruling, as he later wrote in a letter to the Faculty Senate.

It fell to Ms. Wilkinson, a graduate of the university’s law school, to pressure Mr. Ryan to leave. In a June phone call that became heated, she “indicated that the board might even try to fire me for cause if I did not resign,” Mr. Ryan wrote in his letter. He stepped down soon after.

Still, Ms. Wilkinson has hardly been a pushover for the Trump administration. She joined other prominent litigators in signing an amicus brief supporting law firms targeted by the White House last year, and criticized firms that made deals with the administration, her old firm Paul Weiss among them. “I don’t think that’s good for what we’re supposed to stand up for, which is fighting the government and fighting for the rule of law,” she told Bloomberg Law.

She is also representing her former boss Merrick Garland, a named defendant in lawsuits brought by pardoned Jan. 6 rioters seeking compensation from the government.

And then there is the lawsuit by Disney, whose general counsel, David Howard, is a friend and recommended hiring her to help spearhead what may be the biggest test of free speech norms under Mr. Trump. At the District Court hearing in October, Ms. Wilkinson criticized the president for “blatant violations” of the Constitution and derided the administration’s legal rationale that it needed to review ABC’s licenses to prompt better cooperation in a diversity and inclusion employment inquiry.

The attempts to intimidate ABC are “threatening not just to ABC but to all of broadcast media,” she told the judge.

The Trump era may have widened the distance between the warring factions of American politics so much that Ms. Wilkinson and other heirs to Edward Bennett Williams can no longer move easily from one side to the other. “I still believe in that model, where I don’t have to agree with every view that every one of my clients holds,” said Norman Eisen, a former Washington litigator who served as a special counsel to President Barack Obama. “But I understand the views of those who say, ‘Look, in an era of authoritarianism, it’s different.’”

Ms. Wilkinson said in an interview that she had sympathy for companies that had to compromise their principles in order to survive in the Trump era and considered them worthy of representation. Whether she would defend Trump administration officials who may have directly trampled democratic norms, she conceded, she couldn’t say.

The increasingly fraught status of bipartisan fixers and lawyers also reflects the breakdown of an economic and foreign policy consensus that largely held among Washington elites until the first Trump administration, according to Dr. Drutman, the political scientist. The consensus they helped stitch together was not always popular or wise, but it smoothed the way for government action, and its absence helps explain the paralysis that often prevails today. While lawyers like Ms. Wilkinson will probably continue representing clients on both sides of the MAGA divide, Dr. Drutman noted that activists are increasingly trying to choke off this level of promiscuity by demanding purity from lawyers and other middlemen.

And the enforcers appear to be having an effect. Speaking at a conference in March titled “Bending the Knee: How the Legal Establishment and Corporate America Embraced Corruption in the Trump Era,” Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona summed up the mood on the populist left when he argued that lawyers who had collaborated with President Trump or enabled corruption in his administration should be disbarred. Democrats, he added, should blackball them.

The priority is “making sure it’s known that as Democratic senators, these firms that are engaging in this can’t just be hanging out with us as if nothing happened,” Senator Gallego said.

Ms. Wilkinson herself has been on the receiving end of such blowback. In July, a group called the American Economic Liberties Project, which sponsored the “Bending the Knee” conference, took aim at her in a news release about her client Nexstar, an owner of local ABC stations. Critics on the left accuse Nexstar of keeping Jimmy Kimmel off the air for days after ABC lifted his brief suspension over controversial statements in order to cozy up to the Trump administration and win its approval to buy another media company called Tegna. (Nexstar said at the time that it was guided by the sensibilities of the communities it served, “independent of any external influence.”)

After a group of attorneys general accused Nexstar of defying a judicial order to keep the companies separate while they challenged the merger, the American Economic Liberties Project urged the judge to punish executives at Nexstar for violating the order, and to refer Ms. Wilkinson and a colleague for sanctions.

“These are sophisticated actors who know they are actively flouting a judicial order and showing contempt for the court and the rule of law,” a spokesperson for the group said at the time. (Ms. Wilkinson noted in a legal filing that the actions in question were stipulated by Nexstar’s merger agreement and that the company never hid them from public view. Her firm was not sanctioned.)

Asked how Democrats would regard lawyers like Ms. Wilkinson if the party retook the White House in 2028, the group’s executive director, Nidhi Hegde, said some establishment Democrats would most likely praise her defense of ABC against the Trump administration. But, Ms. Hegde said, the case didn’t wash away the stain of her work on behalf of David Ellison and Nexstar.

“If Democrats are serious about actually being a party for working people, then they do really have to take seriously what she’s facilitating with the complete consolidation of media markets,” Ms. Hegde said, alluding to Ms. Wilkinson. “There’s an inherent contradiction in being in lock step with people who facilitate this oligarchy that’s getting more and more powerful.”

John Koblin contributed reporting. Georgia Gee and Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: The Long Life of the ‘Snacking Occasion’
item.description:
Happy hour? That’s a classic “snacking occasion.” Post-workout? An opportunity for a refueling bite. The afternoon cup of coffee that also includes a discounted pastry? That’s another spun-up “snacking occasion.”

Back in the day, three square meals were the standard. Now, many people nibble and snack all day (and night). And shrewd executives are seeking ways to get people to keep spending on all of it, partly by concocting ever more snacking occasions.

The term has been rising in popularity among executives as companies scramble to continue making money through the day even as some consumers shift to smaller portions, or choose snacks in lieu of meals. “Hostess Donettes brand continues to outperform the broader sweet baked goods category,” the chief executive of J.M. Smucker said in August, “reinforcing the brand’s relevance within the A.M. snacking occasion.” Also that month, the El Pollo Loco chief executive said that afternoon and late-night offerings like coffee drinks, chicken tenders and quesadillas were “part of a broader snacking occasion that brings guests into our restaurant outside of traditional mealtime.”

Alex Susskind, a professor at Cornell focused on food and beverage management, said that executives using this term are referring to “a revenue opportunity that exists outside of normal structures.”

The industry term has been around for decades, Mr. Susskind said. But lately, as inflation ruffles consumers’ outlook and the rise of GLP-1 weight loss drugs alters eating patterns, use of the term has picked up. “Snacking occasion” has appeared on 51 conference call transcripts so far in 2026, and was mentioned on 48 transcripts last year, according to Alphasense, a research firm. In the third quarter of this year, the term was used on 20 calls, up from four mentions in the same period a decade earlier.

The ultimate goal of a snacking occasion, Mr. Susskind said, is to “layer in another type of consumption.” Restaurants, of course, want customers to spend lavishly on full meals. But as habits change, brands have tacitly acknowledged that at least some slice of the customer base has a dwindling appetite because of GLP-1 drugs — and they are adjusting offerings accordingly.

“They might actually be subbing out a fuller meal occasion, but you’d rather have them come and snack than have them not come at all,” Mr. Susskind said. Chipotle, for one, now offers meat cups for $4. McDonald’s rolled out more high-protein sides over the summer, and its chief executive said in August that “certainly one of the things that we see with people who go on GLP-1s is they eat more protein,” and “you certainly see portion size go down.”

In recent decades, there has been a “continual graduation of consumers eating differently across the day,” said Sally Lyons Wyatt, who leads food and beverage and snacking research at Circana. Millennials, in particular, began snacking all day long. “GLP-1 is not necessarily cratering the industry,” she added. “It is redefining what consumers are eating.”

The same cup of yogurt can play the role of a full meal or a simple tide-over, depending on the diner’s mind-set. “The product hasn’t necessarily changed, but the role of the product has changed,” Ms. Wyatt added.

“Companies that understand the need behind ‘occasion’ are better positioned than those that think people will stop snacking,” Ms. Wyatt said. After all, she mused, “snacks just aren’t what they used to be.”

item.title: My Co-Worker Is Losing It Over My Religion
item.description:
Send questions about the office, money, careers and work-life balance to workfriend@nytimes.com. Include your name and location, or a request to remain anonymous. Letters may be edited.

Dear Work Friend,

I’m a practicing Buddhist working at a university, with a desk next to a difficult co-worker.

One recent afternoon, while a colleague and a student were talking about a campus event, she loudly wondered whether they’d be “serving Kool-Aid.” The next morning, I found a piece of paper with “the cult” on it taped to her otherwise bare desk, hanging toward my work space.

With H.R.’s blessing, I calmly asked her what the sign meant. She told me to keep her name out of my mouth, mocked my “Karen voice,” and insisted that “the cult is a band!” Since then, she has mimicked my typing, drummed on her desk whenever I stop typing, and moved the sign so it now faces only me.

I reported everything in writing to H.R., which responded that because this co-worker has a pending lawsuit against the university, they can’t take action against her right now, since it could look like retaliation. Their solution was for me to move my desk, but there is no other space.

I don’t want to sue my employer. I just want to come to work without being mocked for my faith. I’m exhausted from managing this on my own while the person causing it faces no consequences.

What can I do when H.R.’s hands seem tied? And how do I keep working next to someone who clearly wants me to feel unwelcome?

Anonymous

Most people are obligated at some point in their careers to work directly adjacent to an unpleasant person. This is frustrating, because “my neighbor sucks as a person” is generally not enough reason to change desks or offices, at least as far as management is usually concerned.

Your bad neighbor, however, has crossed the line into harassment, and done you the favor of giving you leverage. If you’ve made your employers aware that you’re subject to workplace harassment based on your religious practice — as you have — and they’ve done nothing about it — as they have not — you have grounds for a Title VII complaint.

Your H.R. representatives should know this, and if they don’t, your university probably has an equal-opportunity or equity office that can remind their colleagues of their duties. And if it comes to it, I suspect there are a lot of employment lawyers who would be eager to explain to a deep-pocketed university the nuances of Title VII and its obligations to its employees.

The point is that your H.R. reps hands are not tied here. The decision to move you rather than to address the harassment directly is a decision based on legal considerations only insofar as they have determined you are much less likely to sue the university than your co-worker’s lawyer is to file a new motion in her lawsuit. That they reached that decision and still didn’t move you suggests to me that they really, really don’t think you’re going to do anything about it.

I respect that you don’t want to sue your employer. But I don’t think you need to. You just need to make the administration think you might for them to start taking your concerns seriously. Start with a formal letter to your boss, with H.R. CC’ed, including your documentation of the harassment and asking how the university is going to meet its obligations to you.

It doesn’t need to be a threatening letter — but don’t be afraid of escalating to the equal-opportunity or equity office, or of consulting an employment lawyer who might help you draft the kind of letter they’d take seriously. I bet you’d find that all kinds of new office desks will open up to you, ideally with neighbors less interested in English post-punk bands of the 1980s.

Two weeks ago, we published a letter from a woman seeking advice about returning to office work, in her 50s, after two decades of working for herself. We asked Work Friend readers what they would suggest as advice. Across the hundreds of responses, a few clear themes stood out:

Learn to love, or live with, new tech …

By far the most consistent thread among all responses was that workplace tech is entirely unrecognizable, and you’ll need to get up to speed. It’s not just the software you use for your job, but the whole infrastructure of W2 work: “Expect to enroll in benefits, review policies, and sign contracts through payroll and H.R. platforms,” Polly Bangs writes from Portland, Ore. Ron Katz, who returned to office work in his early 60s, advises: “Make friends with the IT and support teams, not just your colleagues. They will save you more quickly than a co-worker who resents or is wary of the new person on the team.”

… especially Slack, Zoom, and GIFs.

New communications software comes with both a learning curve and a new set of expectations. “Don’t expect voice-mail messages to be responded to in a timely manner, if at all,” one writer cautions. Instead, get used to chaotic video conferences. “Remember that guy who went viral in 2017 because his toddler intruded on a BBC interview? That’s how we all work now,” explains another. For style points, “work on your GIF game,” C.A. writes. “People now communicate in GIFs over Slack or Teams.”

Adjust to a new, more casual and more flexible culture …

After technology shock, the second most-mentioned development in the workplace was the rise of more casual dress codes: “It is totally normal to wear tennis shoes on a client call, and I haven’t worn high heels since before Covid,” one reader wrote. The end of suits and ties is accompanied by a broader cultural shift, which one commenter summed up by saying, “Overall, the employment relationship has become less hierarchical and more collaborative.” What sometimes seems like laziness on the part of younger colleagues is often just different habits. Another person writes that his younger colleagues’ flexible hours “doesn’t mean they’re lazy or work less — in my experience, quite the opposite is often true.”

… and be thoughtful in how you communicate.

I’m wording this topline summary carefully, because the advice around this tended to fall into two broad camps: People who believe that young workers today are humorless scolds (“Never make a joke at work” was a common refrain), and people who believe that they’ve struck a blow for better workplaces. (“As a Gen Xer, I give all credit to much-maligned millennials for making the workplace significantly more respectful,” one correspondent writes. On behalf of millennials: Thank you.) Either way, our commenters agreed that caution and thoughtfulness is warranted. “Absolutely everything you say or do at, or even not at, work can be recorded and saved for posterity,” one person wrote.

Be curious and outgoing …

Many people wrote that workplaces are less social than they used to be, and older workers will have to make the first move in establishing relationships. “Moderating my expectations for work friends (haha) was necessary to mitigate my disappointment,” one of our correspondents admitted. But younger workers often appreciate your input, and your curiosity: “If you’re working with a lot of millennials, I’d say lean in. Ask questions, be curious, and share your experience too,” another writer suggests.

… but set boundaries for yourself.

All that new communications tech means it’s harder to leave the workplace. “It’s harder to justify taking a day off when you’re sick because most people can just work from home now,” one person writes. “There’s no such thing as snow days anymore.” For this reason, another commenter advises, “establish early on that you will not be answering work-related calls or emails when off duty.”

Be prepared for a long hiring process …

Many, many readers responded not so much with “workplace advice” as with “job-seeking advice.” “Ageism is very real,” one commenter writes. “Applying for an open position with no connections has very low odds of success.” One 53-year-old woman said she “stopped putting the dates for when I earned my bachelor’s and master’s degrees on my resume and got more responses.”

… and the difficult transition of having a boss again …

Others suggested that the biggest difficulty might be learning how to have a boss again after two decades of working for yourself: “Adjusting to someone else’s processes and priorities may be your biggest challenge,” Melanie Taplett writes. Though there are also some good things: “Relish in not having to do everything yourself,” Ron Katz suggests.

… in fact, maybe don’t do it at all?

A small minority of readers even advised our advice-seeker to avoid returning at all: “‘What advice would you give to someone returning to the office from self-employment?’ Don’t.”

But if you do, there are helpful supplemental materials.

A career counselor in Gainesville had a very specific piece of advice: “Your assignment for today is to rent ‘The Intern’ with Robert De Niro as a traditional worker returning to an office full of young people.”

]]>

item.title: Former ‘60 Minutes’ Boss to Join Video Journalism Start-Up
item.description:
Bill Owens, the former executive producer of “60 Minutes,” left the program last year after clashing with the corporate owners of CBS News. In an emotional meeting announcing his resignation, Mr. Owens said additional layers of oversight had encroached on the independence of the show, a staple of the newsmagazine for decades.

On Thursday, Mr. Owens said he had found a place he could make journalism free from what he viewed as corporate interference: Newpress, a start-up that publishes video journalism from independent creators on YouTube and other digital platforms.

“Legacy media right now is worried about the politics in the country,” Mr. Owens said. “They’re worried about lobbies and sponsorships and advertisers. They’re looking over their shoulder.”

Mr. Owens said he was not interested in that. “I want people to have the truth,” he said.

Mr. Owens, who will become the start-up’s executive producer on March 1 when his noncompete agreement with CBS ends, is joining the company shortly after it raised $12 million from a group of funders led by Emerson Collective, the company founded by the investor and philanthropist Laurene Powell Jobs and the owner of media companies like The Atlantic. The money will be used to produce new shows and explore expansions into newsletters and podcasting, said Iz Harris, chief executive of Newpress.

“The way that we’re going to get there is by doubling down on what we do best,” Ms. Harris said. “Right now, that’s creating shows that are in a creator’s voice and vision that help people understand the broad context of how the world works.”

Over the past decade, the traditional news industry has been disrupted by news creators — journalists who create email newsletters, YouTube videos or podcasts on their own. Newpress takes a hybrid approach, giving news creators some of the research, fact-checking, production and business support offered to journalists in traditional newsrooms. Founded in 2024 by Ms. Harris and her husband, the journalist Johnny Harris, the company recruits journalists who make compelling visual stories and shares the profits with them.

Newpress has hired 20 people, including Max Fisher, who specializes in geopolitics; Christophe Haubursin, whose videos investigate internet mysteries; and Sam Ellis, who makes videos about global sports.

The videos are high-gloss and approachable, with sleek infographics and animations cut together with direct-to-camera narration delivered by journalists in cluttered offices wearing T-shirts and chunky sweaters. One video, on the “oil apocalypse” exacerbated by the continuing war in Iran, featured Mr. Fisher sitting in front of a microphone on a desk with a tiny globe alongside an old, wall-mounted telephone.

In addition to running ads alongside its videos, Newpress sells memberships for $5 per month for subscribers who want to support its journalism and get additional perks. When Mr. Owens starts next year, he will be involved in recruiting more journalists to join Newpress and conceiving and editing stories produced by its creators. He said he was drawn to journalism on YouTube, partly because it was where the next generation of news consumers were spending their time.

“These guys have millions of followers in a demographic that I’ve been chasing for decades,” Mr. Owens said. “My kids are 23 and 24. This is where they find their news and information.”

Other funders in the new round include Glick Family Investments; Jesse Angelo, the chief executive of Checker JP Media; David Leavy, the former chief operating officer of CNN; and Brent Montgomery, the chief executive of Wheelhouse Entertainment. Patrick Steel, the former chief executive of Politico, is investing and will join the board alongside Peter Lattman, the managing director of media at Emerson Collective. Newpress did not disclose its valuation.

item.title: Caryle Murphy Has Died. She Earned a Pulitzer for Reporting in Kuwait.
item.description:
Caryle Murphy, whose intense, monthlong coverage of Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait in 1990 for The Washington Post — an assignment that ended with her escape to Saudi Arabia from Saddam Hussein’s forces — earned her a Pulitzer Prize, died on Oct. 19 in Fairfax County, Va. She was 79.

Her death, in a hospital, was caused by viral pneumonia, her husband, Herbert Howe, said. In 2015, Ms. Murphy had been diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis and three years later received a lung transplant.

Ms. Murphy was The Post’s bureau chief in Cairo in late July 1990, when David Ignatius, the paper’s foreign editor, called to tell her there was reliable information that the Iraqis were likely to invade. At the time, she had a mysterious ailment that left her struggling to stay awake.

“I said, ‘Can you possibly get to Kuwait?’” Mr. Ignatius recalled in an interview. “She got off her sickbed and was one of the few correspondents from American journalism in Kuwait when the tanks rolled in.”

Over four weeks, she reported from Kuwait City about roads littered with burned-out armored cars and trucks; early signs of Kuwaiti resistance; embassies that were under siege; the absence of civil administration; and antiwar protests, mostly by women.

“When someone takes your country,” a Kuwaiti woman told Ms. Murphy, “it’s like tearing out your heart.”

Ms. Murphy felt she was in danger of being rounded up by Iraqi forces and left her hotel to hide in homes, first with Americans and then with Kuwaitis. With phone and Telex lines dead, she had to find other means to send her stories, which included passing them to people leaving Kuwait or rolling them into a tube, with a note identifying herself, and tossing them over the wall of a friendly embassy. The U.S. embassy would not let her use its classified communications channels.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

Some of her stories carried her byline but, after a few days, The Post removed her name to protect her.

She decided to leave Kuwait for several reasons, including not wanting to subject the family that was hiding her to Iraqi threats to hang anyone sheltering a Westerner. One attempt to flee failed. But on Aug. 27, wearing a black veil and robe, she escaped from Kuwait in a nine-vehicle caravan that drove four hours across the desert to Saudi Arabia.

“Stranded cars, left by their occupants, litter the landscape,” she wrote in The Post. “No one talks as our car bounces over the sandy ridges. Three times, we have to stop to dig out one of the vehicles. Two are finally abandoned because their engines died. We meet only two Iraqi soldiers, but they don’t attempt to stop us.”

She remained largely in Saudi Arabia, where in January and February 1991 she covered the Persian Gulf war, in which a military coalition led by the United States liberated Kuwait.

A few months later, she was awarded the Pulitzer for international reporting, which she shared with Serge Schmemann of The New York Times for his coverage of the reunification of Germany.

“It’s really nice to get the mother of all prizes,” Ms. Murphy told The Post newsroom. She also won the George Polk Award for foreign reporting.

Carole Marie Murphy — who change the spelling of her first name in the 1960s to make it more distinctive — was born in Hartford, Conn., on Nov. 16, 1946, and grew up in Brockton, Mass. Her father, Thomas, was a pediatrician, and her mother, Muriel (McCarthy) Murphy, managed the home while raising six children.

In 1968, Ms. Murphy earned a bachelor’s degree in history from Trinity College in Washington (now Trinity Washington University); years later, in 1986, she received a master’s degree in international public policy from the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies.

Looking to travel after her undergraduate degree, she taught English and history for two years at an all-girls’s school in Nyeri, Kenya. Back in the United States, she started her journalism career at The Brockton Enterprise before going back overseas as a freelancer.

In 1976, she was reporting for The Post from Angola — one year after the African country became independent from Portugal but during its civil war — when she was accused by the government of working for the C.I.A. She was placed under house arrest for more than a week, interrogated over her sources for one article and expelled from the country.

She was soon hired full-time by The Post, starting as a suburban reporter in Virginia before being assigned to South Africa from 1977 to 1982. She then returned to cover immigration and other beats.

In 1984, she met Robert Gersony, a consultant to the State Department who told her about mass killings of civilians in Uganda under the strongman leader Milton Obote.

Mr. Gersony had gained no traction within the Reagan administration to intervene to stop the killings, which, she wrote in The Post, were considered by Ugandans and foreign observers “worse than the atrocity-ridden eight-year rule of the country’s former ruler, President Idi Amin.”

The publicity generated by Ms. Murphy’s article “stopped the killings,” Mr. Gersony said in an interview, in part by leading Elliott Abrams, the assistant secretary of state for human rights, to tell the BBC at the time that Uganda no longer had the backing of the United States. The interview was heard around Africa, and Mr. Obote soon met with Chester A. Crocker, the assistant secretary of state for African affairs.

In response to the exposure of the killings, Mr. Gersony recalled, the Obote government opened the Luwero Triangle — the region where the International Committee of the Red Cross estimated that more than 300,000 people were killed — to relief operations.

“The government delegitimized itself with its actions,” Mr. Gersony said. “And Caryle’s article was the vehicle for breaking the Obote government,” which fell in a bloodless military coup in 1985.

Ms. Murphy joined The Post’s Cairo bureau in 1989 and reported from the Middle East for five more years, before moving to the religion beat. After taking a buyout from the paper in 2006, she returned to Saudi Arabia two years later as a freelancer for The Christian Science Monitor and other publications.

As a public policy scholar at the Wilson Center, she researched and wrote “A Kingdom’s Future: Saudi Arabia Through the Eyes of Its Twentysomethings” (2013). It was her second book, following “Passion for Islam: Shaping the Modern Middle East: The Egyptian Experience” (2002). She also wrote about religion for the Pew Research Center.

In addition to her husband, whom she married in 2017, Ms. Murphy is survived by two sisters, Karen Burke and Colleen Kirchgessner; and two brothers, Kevin and Kenan Murphy.

In one of her final dispatches from Kuwait, in August 1990, Ms. Murphy wrote in a first-person story that a week before the Iraqi invasion, Mr. Hussein’s “bullying rhetoric and even his huge military buildup on the border, still seemed like distant, familiar rumbles to most Kuwaitis.

“Invasion? ‘Forget it,’ they said. ‘We’ve heard all this before from Iraq.’”

Everything still seemed normal, she wrote. The city’s beaches were crowded, and the Kuwaiti military had not been placed on alert, for fear that Mr. Hussein would be provoked.

“It was,” she wrote, “a fatal mistake.”

item.title: Elizabeth Holmes Gives a Batman Villain a Run for His Money
item.description:
It was villain versus villain at the weekend box office, with a shape-shifting comic-book menace facing an unexpectedly formidable challenger: Elizabeth Holmes.

“Clayface,” an R-rated horror movie about a lesser-known Batman villain, was No. 1 at North American theaters. It took in about $24 million from Thursday night through Sunday, according to Rentrak, which compiles box office data. “Clayface” was inexpensive to make, at least by superhero standards. Warner Bros. and its DC Studios division spent $44 million on the film, which received mostly positive reviews.

The “Clayface” opening was modest — at the low end of prerelease analyst expectations. For DC, however, it was a relief. The studio’s “Supergirl” was a box office disaster in July, taking in $126 million worldwide against production and marketing costs of at least $270 million. (Studios typically split ticket sales 50-50 with theaters.)

Warner Bros. said “Clayface” collected an additional $19 million overseas, for a global opening total of about $43 million.

Coming in a surprisingly close second in North America was Ms. Holmes, playing herself. “You Can See Everything,” a nearly three-hour documentary about the disgraced Theranos founder, collected roughly $20 million in its second weekend, for a new domestic total of about $45 million. Demand has been so strong that A24 expanded the film to 2,655 theaters, an exceptionally wide release for a documentary and more than triple its opening-weekend footprint.

A24 spent less than $10 million to produce “You Can See Everything.” The marketing campaign, which relied heavily on internet memes, cost a similar amount.

Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, “You Can See Everything” is the highest-grossing nonmusical documentary since Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11” in 2004. Reviews have been breathless, with one critic calling it “unmissable.” Oscar prognosticators are treating “You Can See Everything” as a serious contender for a best picture nomination, which would be a first for a documentary.

Greg Durkin, the founder of Enact Insight, an entertainment research firm, said in a report that “You Can See Everything” had mobilized 20-something and infrequent moviegoers by exploring “identity delusion” and “performative authenticity.” In the film, Ms. Holmes presents herself as a wide-eyed idealist whose ambitions were misunderstood, rather than a convicted fraudster who lied and lied.

“Fahrenheit 9/11” (Lionsgate) holds the box office record for a nonmusical documentary. It sold $119 million in tickets at North American theaters by the end of its run, or about $212 million after adjusting for inflation. As of Sunday, “You Can See Everything” ranked as the sixth-highest-grossing nonmusical documentary in Hollywood history, after adjusting for inflation, a whisper behind the 2012 right-wing film “2016: Obama’s America.”

For all its success, “You Can See Everything” has yet to approach the box office frenzy of “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which rode a wave of anger over the Iraq war. Mr. Moore’s polemic collected $55.5 million from 1,725 theaters after its second weekend in the summer of 2004, or about $98.7 million in today’s dollars.

Rounding out the weekend’s top three was “Wildwood,” directed by Travis Knight and produced by Laika, the Oregon stop-motion animation studio founded by his father, the Nike co-founder Phil Knight. “Wildwood,” about a teenage girl who searches an enchanted forest for her kidnapped brother, debuted to about $11 million, comfortably above prerelease analyst expectations. But the film, which received rave reviews, was expensive to make. It cost about $100 million, not including marketing.

In semi-limited release, the romantic fable “Wicker,” starring Olivia Colman as a lonely fisherwoman who commissions a basket maker to create her a husband (Alexander Skarsgard), took in a solid $6 million for Black Bear, a film company founded by Teddy Schwarzman, son of the billionaire financier Stephen A. Schwarzman.

The Spanish-language film “La Bola Negra,” which Netflix acquired at the Cannes Film Festival, expanded to nine theaters in its second weekend and generated about $245,000 in ticket sales, for a new total of $650,104. Netflix is giving the well-reviewed “La Bola Negra” an exclusive 45-day theatrical run, the longest such window in the streaming giant’s history.

Dead on arrival was “Klara and the Sun,” a science-fiction drama about an artificial intelligence companion purchased to comfort a sickly teenage girl. Starring Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams and directed by Taika Waititi, the $20 million movie collected $725,000 from 880 theaters for Sony Pictures Entertainment and Spyglass Media Group.
